Description

PGE2 acting on the EP3 receptor couples to Gi, which inhibits adenylate cyclase and lowers cAMP, the opposite of the Gs-coupled EP2 and EP4 receptors. In inflamed joints EP3 activation on primary sensory neurons is largely antinociceptive and counteracts PGE2 sensitisation, though spinal EP3 can contribute to hyperalgesia at low PGE2 doses. EP3 is present in the joint nerves of patients with painful osteoarthritis, which makes its signalling direction important to draw correctly.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

Here PGE2 and EP3 are blue. EP3 couples to Gi and lowers cAMP, and an EP3 agonist relieved pain in inflamed knee joints of rats, acting on peripheral and spinal nociceptive neurons. EP3 is present in the joint nerves of patients with painful OA (Natura 2013). The same PGE2 is red in the EP1, EP2 and EP4 blocks: its net effect on the nociceptor is the balance of these receptors, which in inflammation favours sensitisation.
